utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put the same question to you, General Talic: Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner and Nicholas Koumjian, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman and I appear with Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And appearances for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I am Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic. I am replacing Maitre Pitron and Maitre de Roux, and I'm assisted by Mr. Fabien Masson. I would also like to apologise on behalf of Maitre de Roux and Maitre Pitron and I would like to ask you to permit me to represent General Talic and Mr. Brdjanin until next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. General Talic, Maitre de Roux last Friday, or whenever it was -- when did we sit last? Last Wednesday. Last Wednesday, stated in this Trial Chamber, in this courtroom, that you had no objection in being represented today by Mademoiselle Fauveau. Do you confirm that? And now since we have a statement being made by Mademoiselle Fauveau to the effect that, until next Tuesday, in other words until today week, none of your two appointed counsel will be present. Do you still accept that you will be represented by Mademoiselle Fauveau between now and then? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I still agree to that and I accept being represented by Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, simply this, the -- tomorrow, as Your Honour knows, it was intended to deal with the admissibility of the Banja Luka documents. Now, it may be that as a result of the very productive Status Conference that was held with your senior legal officer, that things will be shortened. But nonetheless, it is a matter in which counsel for General Talic have raised a number of objections and tomorrow is the time when Your Honours will be asked to rule on the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will rule, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The second matter is this: On Monday, the two witnesses who are coming, one of them I know gives direct evidence - it depends on the second - will be giving direct evidence of a meeting with General Talic. Now, I don't know whether that was appreciated. If one looked at the list, it should have been, but I merely raise that so that General Talic is aware that it may be on Monday we will be reaching a witness who will be giving direct evidence in respect of a meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, and I can assure you that this Trial Chamber - I don't even need to consult my two colleagues - appreciates very much your sense of loyalty both to the Chamber and to your colleagues on the other side. I'm sure that Ms. Fauveau has understood perfectly well what you stated and the import of what you stated and that she will refer back to Maitre de Roux and Maitre Pitron so that they will decide what to do. I mean, it's up to them. This Trial Chamber is definitely not -- what I must make clear is that the office and the Registry in charge of the allocation of Defence counsel, et cetera, are fully aware of what is taking place and there may well be -- come a stage when the undesired might happen. We can't simply -- we can't go on like this. This is, again, not a reflection on you. You are perfectly capable of handling the situation, but the two lawyers that have been allocated at an expense to your client, to General Talic, are Maitre de Roux and Maitre Pitron. And from Maitre Pitron, at least for the time being, there has not been an explanation justifying his absence except what Maitre de Roux said that he is somehow engaged in a case in a court of Avignon or at Aix-en-Provence or something like that. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have decided, after consultation with a number of colleagues, that I need to place something on the record regarding this issue that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is far from clear in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that a waiver by an accused of the appearance of counsel assigned to him would be seen as knowing, intelligent and effective, and I therefore have serious concern that this issue could very well cause significant delay at some point in this case, or even cause the case to have to be completely restarted. With that in mind, I would just like to preliminarily ask the Chamber to seriously consider, if that were to occur, to sever my case from his so that we can go forward and not be subjected to that delay, but I believe it is very inappropriate for counsel assigned by the Registry to an accused in a genocide case of this magnitude to not be appearing in court. And I would hope that it would not affect the continuation of my client's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I can assure you that it will not affect the continuation of your client's case. I think the more I hear about this matter, the more I'm convinced that it would benefit everyone if it's brought to a head. If you would like to file an appropriate motion, we will deal with it and I can assure you that this Trial Chamber will bring it at a head and in the speediest manner and in the most forceful manner. And then, of course, there will be a price to pay. Now, yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only like to say -- to provide you with an explanation, in order to avoid problems of this kind in the future. In fact, our cabinet did not receive counsel at the beginning of this case so we worked in an organisation, in a particular organisation. In fact, there were three of us who were dealing with this case. We were dealing with it as the principal, the main counsel. It was only a few months ago that we were designated ex officio and we have only had a few months to adapt to the procedure of this Tribunal. I would assure you that this cabinet, that we are doing all we can to resolve this question as soon as possible. And until that time, I would be grateful if you could authorise me to represent General Talic because he doesn't object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a question of authorising you or not authorising you. I said before, and I reiterate it, you are perfectly capable of handling the situation and of representing General Talic. That has never been the issue. That has never been doubted. That has never been questioned by anyone. The whole point is this: The whole point is that there are two lawyers that have been appointed by the Registrar to represent General Talic. The moment they were appointed, they assumed obligations and responsibilities not only with regard to their client but also in relation to this Trial Chamber. I made a very specific warning or I gave a very specific warning earlier on last week, that if this, at any moment, threatens to bring this trial to a halt, even temporarily, your Defence bench will not even know what would have happened. I will hit hard before you even know it. And I'm telling you also that the Registry, the Registrar, and the person responsible for the office of appointing lawyers, is already fully aware of the situation. There may come a time when there will be a price to pay and the price will certainly not include having this trial halted, not even temporarily, but we may come to that stage. This is intolerable. If, for example - let me make it clear - if Maitre Pitron finding himself engaged in a surprise trial or proceedings in Avignon or Aix-en-Provence, decided that his place is there and not here, he has to justify in front of this Trial Chamber why, in this particular case, where he is being paid by the funds of the Tribunal itself, he has opted to have you, someone else, not on the record as being one of counsel for General Talic, to represent General Talic, and he hasn't opted to do the same in that urgent case that he has in Avignon or in Aix-en-Provence. This is what I'm trying to make clear. This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I interrupt Your Honour? There is one thing. In fact, to my knowledge, Maitre Pitron is not actually on the list. They were originally both retained by General Talic privately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's true, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the order, when it came out, assigning them whatever the Tribunal equivalent of legal aid is, only mentions Mr. de Roux. So it's fair to say Mr. Pitron is not registered as counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not even registered as counsel either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know how it's been worked out but on the notification we got, it merely talked about Mr. de Roux.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will have that checked because the information I was given was somehow different. That actually, when the private brief that they had was terminated, I got the impression that both of them were retained then by the Registry. I will have that checked. Obviously, if it is as you say, it will change a little bit the picture as far as Maitre Pitron is concerned, but certainly not as far as Maitre de Roux is concerned. And the situation cannot be allowed to remain as it is. I mean, definitely not. Because I have enough experience behind me to realise that this could create a very, very awkward and embarrassing and complicated situation for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic may stand up at some point in time and say, "Listen, I was forced, I had no option." So, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner is right. Maitre Pitron has still not been officially designated as counsel, and according to the proposals from our office, we are looking for a solution to make sure everything is according to regulations by next week. My only request at the moment is to know whether I'm authorised to represent General Talic until next Tuesday, and I promise that after that date, the matter will be ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You can go ahead and you're being authorised to represent General Talic simply because General Talic, upon being asked, made the declaration that was put on record earlier on. Thank you. Now, I understand there will be some issues with regard to procedure and whatever that may have to be discussed. Incidentally, yesterday, I went through the draft decision on the guidelines which will govern the procedure in the course of this trial which I had delivered orally earlier on. It should be -- very few corrections that had to be made. It should be out and handed down to you later on today. So that should settle the matter. If there are other things that you would like to have discussed, of course, they will be discussed. However, I was going to suggest to you to finish first with the witness so that we make sure that he won't -- his presence won't be required here in The Hague any further, and then presumably we will have ample time or sufficient time to deal with the rest, if that is agreeable to you. If there is something urgent that you would like to have discussed first and foremost before everything else, then please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I was assuming that tomorrow would be, as it were, a sort of mopping up day, if that's the right expression. May I just, however, mention one thing? Your Honours will have seen in the record, I hope, of the Status Conference that we discussed the legal argument about the dead witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it was the view of Madam Fauveau that would be better dealt with at a later stage as well, and that's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw actually the minutes of the meeting that took place which, as I anticipated, would be thoroughly positive one and I'm positive future ones will even be more productive. Yes, I have taken note of that and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours are agreeable to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course. So yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one, and this may have resulted from total confusion on my part but I would like to inquire as a matter of the record -- in the witness's statement of 10-14 December, 10, 12 and 14, 15 February, at page 20, the witness indicates that he's been shown an English translation of his book, consisting of 160 pages, and I think we have only been given 82 pages, unless I'm just totally confused and -- but it was my understanding what we were given were 82 pages but I thought I understood it until I started looking at it again this morning, and now I'm not sure I do. So maybe the Prosecutor can fill us in on that but I think we were given 82 pages when the witness says he had 160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you there but perhaps Mr. Koumjian can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was that the 95 statement? Which statement was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We can check on that. In fact, I could ask and send an e-mail and ask someone to print out that range, but as far as I know, it's only 81 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could well be that the witness will turn up with a copy himself. I mean, was it given to him to keep or during the course of his evidence? Because I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was given to him to keep, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were heading towards parity of arms with Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's why I get along so well with him because I understand the problems. I have them myself. As far as I know, I have the range that we printed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, it's not something --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's probably a matter of the print that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It also may be printed on both sides and that explains because we are talking of 82 and 160, so it could well be that. So can we call the witness? Please bring the witness in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I've just been informed that the discrepancy is due to one is a draft translation. That was the number referred to by the witness, and the ERN range Mr. Ackerman has that begins 01901083 is the final translation which comes to 82 pages, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krzic. You are now going to be requested to make the same declaration, solemn declaration that you made on earlier occasions. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down, thank you. Mr. Ackerman will be continuing with his cross-examination. And you are kindly invited to -- and you are kindly invited to keep your answers as brief and as to the point as possible. I remind you of what I told you last week, that just as you made a solemn declaration to say the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, in answering questions or in giving testimony, basically, you should answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question. That would make the Trial Chamber much happier and also Mr. Ackerman will have less opportunity of firing further questions to you. Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask that the witness be again given copies of his various statements so that we can refer to them during his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you enlighten me on that? Is he in possession of them or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have them here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have them, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps -- we have labelled again the statements, statement 1, 2, 3 and 4, starting with the 1995 and the last one, so it might be easier to direct his attention by the number of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krzic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How are you today? We are still on statement number 1, and I'd ask you -- well, I'll get there in a moment. But I'll ask you to turn to a certain page in just a moment. I want to talk about the referendum, and you know what I'm referring to when I talk about the referendum, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're talking about the referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And that was a referendum that was conducted through voting on secret ballots, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, secret ballot means that the name of the voter is not on the ballot so you never can know who voted for or against that proposition, can you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, but I did not participate in practical terms in the implementation of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you don't know that there would be any records that would let me find out how you voted in that referendum. There wouldn't be, would there, if they are secret ballots?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only way I'd know how you voted is if I asked you and you decided you wanted to tell me, but you could also choose not to tell me, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And anyone who was any kind of an active politician during that period of time would have understood what secret ballots were about and how secret ballots worked, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that -- let me refer you now to page 28 of your statement. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first English version?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Number 1, page 28, about two-thirds of the way through the last paragraph on the page. You say, "Mr. Brdjanin announced that those who voted for an independent BH would be dismissed from their jobs." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I don't see it, I agree with that, but as far as I know --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a pretty ridiculous statement, isn't it, because there is no way he could have found out who voted for an independent BH if the balloting was by secret ballot; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think that this refers to the Serbian plebiscite, at which the SDS required that all Serbs take part, especially the leaders, and those ballots were available and I think that this refers to that plebiscite or referendum as you're calling it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm actually referring to what you call the referendum and that whole paragraph, if you start at the top of that paragraph, and read, it begins with, "When the referendum was held in Banja Luka." It doesn't speak of the plebiscite, it speaks of the referendum. Doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that, to the best of my recollection, and I think I refer to that referendum in this book, it is very easy for me to establish what this is about, so that actually Mr. Brdjanin's statement refers to the Serb referendum that they had held previously. Maybe in the translation, this confusion may have been made so that the references to the referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina but in fact it relates to the referendum of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you start with the first sentence, "When the referendum was held in Banja Luka, the result was that 45 per cent of the municipal population wanted an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now that refers to the referendum, not the plebiscite, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That refers to the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The town of Banja Luka, the vote for an independent BH was 65 per cent, meaning that the number of Serbs in the town, that a number of Serbs in the town voted in favour of it. That refers to the referendum, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there must be something wrong here. Whether it is due to the translation or not, I don't know. 45 per cent refers to the city of Banja Luka. That is the percentage that voted in favour of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. 65 per cent applies to the level of the whole state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the actual percentage, I was saying that 45 per cent of the total population of the municipality of Banja Luka voted in favour, and out of the number that voted, I think 98 or 99 per cent also voted in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask the question again and perhaps this time you can answer it. In the town of Banja Luka, the vote for an independent BH was 65 per cent, meaning that a number of Serbs in the town voted in favour of it. That refers, does it not, to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sentence here, there is one or two words that have been inserted incorrectly, and I repeat, 45 per cent or maybe a couple of figures higher than that, but you have the official numbers, in the town of Banja Luka or rather the municipality of Banja Luka, voted in favour of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, but you need to know that only the non-Serbs took part in the vote and as part of the Serbs, so another figure that is lacking is that about 98 per cent of the total number of voters who voted, 98 or 99 per cent voted in favour of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and which in relation to the total population is 45 per cent. If you take into account the fact that a certain number of people did not vote at all, for various reasons, which is not relevant for you, I repeat, 65 per cent applies to Bosnia-Herzegovina as the whole state, and these are very well-known figures. There is no need to enter into a polemics about that. There is nothing I can change about that. These are figures that have been established by the official authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me try a third time. I'm referring to the second sentence which begins with the language, "In the town." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My only question is this: Does that sentence refer to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, but the figure refers to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not to the town of Banja Luka, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's go to the next sentence. "I ran the referendum in practically all of Bosanska Krajina as the authorised envoy of the BH government." That sentence refers to the referendum, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in the whole of Bosanska Krajina. I led the referendum in the territory of the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you not say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that sentence? Where have you got it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the very next sentence. It's the third sentence in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how come that mistake was made. It is true that there is my -- I don't know what you call it, not my signature but whatever, that is true. But I cannot claim to have done something I didn't do. There is no point in saying that I covered the whole territory when that was not officially, or in practical terms, the case but I did meet with the observers who covered the whole region and who were based in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do see at the bottom of that page what appears to be your signature. It says, "signed," and then after that some writing appears to be your signature?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next sentence: "The international observers who came to Banja Luka were organised by me." Now, those were observers of the referendum, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll skip a sentence and go to the next one after that which begins, "In this referendum, old differences were forgotten and even members of family proscribed as nationalist Serbs voted in favour of an independent BH. That sentence refers to the referendum, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next sentence, "Mr. Brdjanin announced that those who voted for an independent BH would be dismissed from their jobs." Are you wanting to tell this Trial Chamber that at that point you started talking about the plebiscite and not the referendum? Or doesn't that also refer to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That refers to the Serb plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course that would be clear to anybody reading it, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that very clearly in my book, and you can find that statement on page 73 of the 21st of November, 1991, I think it is. Yes, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Serb plebiscite that you talk about was also voting by secret ballot, with no opportunity for anyone to know who voted for or against it, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, it was a question of registering the voters, whether they registered for the plebiscite, whether they took part in the vote. So those lists were accessible to the authorities in power at the time, so it was a locally covered plebiscite. That is what is referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're saying is that it was possible to determine whether someone had voted but not possible to determine how they had voted, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that Mr. Brdjanin said those who voted in favour of an independent BH would be dismissed from their jobs, there was no way he could have known that because it was a secret ballot. He could only have known who actually voted in the plebiscite if that's what we are talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we had in mind that with the election results, one knew that manipulation was possible, that those who had the right to have access to the electoral lists, they also had the ability to influence the results. That is how we believed. That is the conclusion that can be made from this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn now, if you would, to your third statement, which is the statement 10 and 14 December, which actually -- December of 2000 and February of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll just start at the beginning and work our way through. Now, by December 2000 and February 2001, you know, do you not, that Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Talic have now been indicted and arrested and are detained in The Hague awaiting trial?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really assume that is correct but I cannot remember such details now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The investigators from the Prosecutor's office are specifically interested in questioning you about these two individuals, are they not, at this point?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot claim any such thing but that can best be seen from the statements whether those things were focused on or not, but I cannot now remember those statements in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it at this time that you asked the Prosecutor's office to assist you in getting some property in Banja Luka returned to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you discuss that with the Prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just complained that my property was not being returned to me because I was testifying, not just my property but that of my entire close family members, and that, in fact, the legal rulings that exist in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not being implemented with respect to my property and the property of my closest relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't the Prosecutor's office agree to assist you in getting that property returned to you and your closest relatives?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's office just said that they would have that in mind. Whether they actually did anything, I don't know. Anyway, nothing has been returned to me or my relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it was because you were testifying. How did anyone know you were testifying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my book was sufficient in that respect, and secondly, it is well known that my testimonies are -- I even mention them in this book, that my attitude towards the Tribunal was fully transparent to the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've not testified in the Tribunal before, have you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about cooperation with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know that the fact that your property hasn't been returned has anything to do with whether you're testifying in this Tribunal or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Testifying at this Tribunal is a matter of honour and of course it has nothing to do with my property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the last you were told by the Prosecutor's Office about the return of your property?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see in practice that no one has done anything in that respect, and I assume it would have been very easy to do that in view of the fact that I have highest level rulings, including those on human rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a ruling by the ombudsman, and I have those decisions in my possession for several years and nothing has been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this particular meeting with the investigators from the Prosecutor's office, you were asked about the Crisis Staff, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at page 3, the third paragraph, what you told the investigators was that when the Crisis Staff was initially set up, it included members of the SDA, HDZ, SDP and the Reformist Party. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told them that the representative of the SDA on the Crisis Staff was Emir Dzanic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in the Council of National Defence, which later developed into the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you find for me where on page 3 you called it the Council of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, assumes facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? Could you repeat your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: He asked him to find where he says it's national defence, and that's assuming that it does say that on the page, and I think perhaps his question is, "Did you say that on there?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Koumjian is right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at that page and tell me if on that page you ever referred to the Council of National Defence? Are you looking?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't know you were speaking to me. I thought you were talking to the Prosecution. I'm sorry. I see now there is no mention of the Council of National Defence there and I'm sorry that this has happened in the statement, but in the book, it is correct, and you should know that the interviews I was exposed to happened subsequently and it is quite possible that certain synonyms may have provoked a certain discrepancy, as you call it, but it is quite clearly stated until when Mr. Djanic and other members of other parties were members of the Council of National Defence or rather when they ceased being members of their own free will. You can find that in the book. You asked me about information where various things could be found and you even photocopied those pages and so I would appeal to you to use that information as I have been using it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this statement was made last -- in December of 2000 and February of 2001. You acknowledged that it was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection, and signed it, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't use my book then, which is the most -- the best document. I thought these statements were more of a formal nature and -- when it comes to things like this, the Crisis Staff and Council of National Defence, that both you and the Prosecution would have the precise data as to when, what happened, and you can find that clearly stated in the book. You can find the page where it is said why members of the other parties left the Council of National Defence and when it became the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Ackerman, and witness, please, Mr. Krzic. Mr. Ackerman, may I refer you to the previous page, last paragraph? The witness obviously had a full weekend in which he could have re-read not only his book but also his statements. "It is difficult to recall the exact date when I first heard the expression 'Krizni Stab' (Crisis Staff). I believe the phrase Crisis Staff was first used from a military standpoint, 'Savjet narodne obrane' (National Defence Council) which was set up in Banja Luka in response to the war in Croatia. This body was formed sometime in 1991 under the normal 'parliamentary life in Banja Luka'. Around this Bosniaks and Croats had already started to face difficulties in the municipal assembly. In the assembly proceedings Bosniaks were openly referred to as 'Turks' and Croats as 'Ustashas'." So basically the explanation the witness is giving as to the confusion that might on the face of it appear is more or less justified in the eyes of this Trial Chamber, so I would suggest that you -- unless you have other reasons why you should continue questioning on this point, I would suggest that you move to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDA representative on this group was a gentleman named Emir Dzanic, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there came a time, did there not, when this group, whether it be called a Crisis Staff or a National Defence Council, decided to visit the border areas, municipalities, bordering Croatia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that decision, but as for the actual moment, I would have to look it up in my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you recall that, do you recall that there was a protest from the SDA to that visit on the grounds that this Crisis Staff had no jurisdiction outside of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this protest and such a view, as far as I can remember, was publicly stated by the SDA party on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you believe that Predrag Radic was the initial president of this Crisis Staff or whatever you want to call it, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was the president of the municipality at the time, and at that time, he was responsible for the president of the -- as president of the Council of National Defence. That was the first thing. And as things developed later on in the Crisis Staff with regard to authority, I described this to the extent that I had knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with regard to these meetings, these visits to the municipalities bordering Croatia, you say that Mesud Islamovic, who was then the president of the SDA, publicly denounced those visits. My question is, is this the same Islamovic who later served in the BH assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he denounced the proclamation of the state of emergency in the municipality, for reasons which I can tell you about, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know if this is also the same Islamovic who you mentioned with regard to the Vance-Owen meetings that you had?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person that you called a collaborator?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't call him a collaborator?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at your first statement again, the one, number 1, at page 15 --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the heading "Meeting Vance and Owen," if you go down two sentences, it says: "I prepared a small SDA delegation and went to see them in the Hotel Bosna." Meaning Vance and Owen. "The Serbs had wanted to prepare a great meal for them but Mr. Vance had declined. Mr. Islamovic, a representative in the BH assembly, was already in the room with Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, and he did not agree with my delegation coming as well. I call him a collaborator. He never said that something wrong happened in Banja Luka. When he was given chances later, he never said the truth." Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that he was a collaborator. A cooperator, to say. I don't know how my statement in B/C/S was translated into English but I think that in my statement, it said that he risked being Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. such a person. I would like to be able to see that statement of mine. I have to say that the English statements that I have initialed, I haven't had the time to read through them. I didn't know that such precision was going to be demanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you also have the B/C/S version of your statement and this particular section begins on page 11 of that statement. And probably the best thing for you to do is read that -- just read that out loud where it starts with "Gospodin Islamovic." Just read that part out loud and let the translators translate it properly so we will know exactly what it does say.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is this on, the reference to Islamovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do keep in mind that the Trial Chamber is not do -- does not have before it the B/C/S version, to start with. But in any case, I wanted to know what your objection was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour if the Court understands the procedure, I think that this exercise would not be relevant, because the statement of the witness is taken only in English. The witness is never given a statement in B/C/S to read. The statement is then, for the purposes of discovery, translated back in The Hague into B/C/S. So the words in B/C/S that Mr. Krzic is going to read is something that a translator wrote from the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But was he interviewed in English or was he interviewed in -- Ms. Korner was -- no, not Ms. Korner in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: She was present -- no, not on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What I can tell the Court is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The procedure is, and I believe Mr. Krzic can verify whether this occurred at the time, is that he's interviewed with an interpreter. However, the statement is written by the investigator or attorney there in English and then read back by the interpreter into B/C/S, and the witness is asked to sign it. That's the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, that convinces me more and more to allow the question to be put as it has been put and the witness to answer it the way it has -- because if the interview took place in B/C/S and was translated into English, and the witness made to sign a statement which is in the English language, presumably, we all have experience of this. I don't believe that this was read out to him word-for-word in the English language. If it was read out word-for-word to him, it would have been in his own language. So basically, I mean, if there is a B/C/S version of what his statement was, I mean, we should let him read it and we should have it translated. Basically, what it's going to change, I don't know. If you ask me, I don't think it's going to change much. I mean, the purpose of Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination at this point in time and for the whole duration of the past hour, has been to try and show the Trial Chamber that some of the things that the witness said in his statement are such that he should not be held to be a reliable witness, or at least that he falls into contradictions or he makes haphazard statements without -- anyway, I mean I think we could go ahead with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just wanted the Trial Chamber to be aware that this is not his original statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is very important for me to know, definitely, but I think we need to go ahead with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps in light of that, I'd like to change it just slightly, Your Honour. Let me try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, stick to it now because the Trial Chamber wants the witness to read himself what he has in front of him and the interpreters to translate what he would be reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, it's on page 11 of the B/C/S version of the statement, beginning with "Gospodin Islamovic." Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the English statement, but my lawyer warned me that on page 10 or 11, this conversation is referred to on that page, the conversation with the co-presidents, and this is in the Bosnian version. In the Bosnian version, I can't find the statement that is contained in the English version, if it is referring to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you will look on page 11 of the B/C/S statement, it says, "Sobi sa g. Vanceom i g. Owenon," if I can speak that language at all in an understandable way. And then halfway through that paragraph, you will see "Gospodin Islamovic." And I also see the word "kolaboracionistom," which I guess probably means "collaborator," but I'd like to you read, beginning where it says, "Gospodin Islamovic," down through where it begins "Gospodin Rodic." Do you find that? You have to look at the last paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The page 11? Which page are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 11 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. The part that I've highlighted in yellow.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is on page 10 and you mentioned page 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mine says page 10, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any lawyer embarking on a good cross-examination is always one page ahead of the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just read the part that I've outlined in yellow, please, out loud?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mr. Islamovic, a representative in the BH assembly, was already in the room with Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, and he did not agree with my delegation coming. I called him a collaborationist."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the present or in the past?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, but I don't have this in my text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does the witness not have in his text?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is very curious. He has a different B/C/S statement than I was given, apparently. I can't explain that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would also like the witness to explain whether -- could I again have that document shown on my monitor, please? Yes. The words "nazvao sam ga kolaboracionistom." Is that in the present tense or in the past tense? Because the translator, the interpretation, was, "I called him." While the version in English that we have in the statement is, "I call him." And it makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the version that I have, it has neither the one nor the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't have the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this version, in the Bosnian version that I have in front of me, I don't have that sentence. I'm confused. Please check this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber would like to see the version, the document, that you have in front of you which, according to you, does not contain this part of the statement. Is this document which you handed to him this morning or is it something that he brought him, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's something that we handed to him this morning that was actually printed last week. If I could just ask the Court perhaps we could check the ERN numbers to check to see if the documents are the same. It's possible there are different translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I would like the document to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask the interpreters to translate to me or to us the word "redigovano."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Revised," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I have a suspicion that the document that the witness had in front of him, and to which he was referring, is a draft, which may have been submitted to him before the final version was presented for his signature, because all along, you have this "/redigovano /redigovano /redigovano," and I would like some sort of explanation... [Microphone not activated] It's unacceptable to have supposedly the same document in two different versions. I mean, this document that Mr. Ackerman provided the witness certainly does not have these "/redigovano /redigovano," while the other one that the witness had in front of him does certainly have this word recurring almost, not in every line, but almost in every line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it could mean "redacted" too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know but I certainly would require or would ask for an explanation at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can give you my present state of mind explanation and I can verify it at the break but, Your Honour, when translations are done, they are usually done in draft and then the final version, the final version is checked by a certified interpreter, certified by the Registry. And apparently, from what Your Honour is saying, it appears that there is two different versions. Mr. Ackerman probably has the final and the witness was given apparently the draft. I think one of the ways we can verify that is by the ERN number, and if the ERN begins with an "L," then I believe it's a draft translation. If they both have the same ERN number, it should be the same document. If they have different ERN numbers, then it's different translations but, again, both are translations from the original and the witness never signs any document in B/C/S. He would not have seen this before he came to the Hague in B/C/S because when he's interviewed only in English, the statement is taken. That is read back to him by an interpreter orally, who translates it into B/C/S, but the witness is never given at the time of the interview a B/C/S version to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, please do check on this because it is important. In the first page of the document that the witness had in front of him, at the bottom of the page, there is a "potpis/paraf redigovano" between a slash and a slash, and then further on is "osvjedoceno/potpisano/potpisano," if that could help you understand better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If Your Honour wants to take the break now, I'll make sure we get the same document in front of the witness that Mr. Ackerman has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a very good idea, Mr. Koumjian. I'm sure Mr. Ackerman agrees to that as well. I'm handing back these two documents to the witness, and we will take it up from there after the break. Please do come forward with some kind of explanation. Thank you. --- Break taken at 10.22 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Could you bring the witness in again, please? Thank you. Before we start, there is a short communication that I would like to make on my behalf and also on behalf of the other two Judges. Towards the end of today's sitting, there will be a ruling given with regard to the representation of General Talic. It will be an important ruling which will be followed up immediately the moment we have reason to take further action. I have checked with regard to Maitre Pitron. The information that you gave to this Tribunal is more or less correct. However, Maitre Pitron is not on record as co-counsel, because he has not yet furnished the required information with regard to his qualifications that would make him accepted as co-counsel. However, he is being paid to act as co-counsel when he appears, when he makes an appearance, and he -- in other words, there is an implicit and direct acknowledgement of his role as co-counsel. And the Tribunal -- the Trial Chamber will certainly not allow any games to take place. We are going to put our foot down starting from today. There will be no further dilly-dallying in this matter. We are going to give a ruling. Ms. Fauveau, please do not take it as a reflection on you. You've got nothing to do with this. The Trial Chamber has also been given the advice not to give you permission to represent General Talic. For the present moment, given the declaration that General Talic himself made this morning, and not having any reason to doubt that General Talic is not being forced to make such a declaration, you will be allowed to represent him today, and after today, I don't know what the situation is going to be but certainly we are going to put our foot down. And towards the end of the sitting, we will come down with a ruling. Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, in that situation, I think that I cannot continue to represent him even today, because this is a rather difficult situation for me and I am under obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, I have to interrupt you. You will not be allowed to do that. You made -- you entered a declaration today. Maitre de Roux entered a declaration last Wednesday, and I am repeating to you now in open court, we will not tolerate any games. Please sit down and let's go ahead. And then everybody will suffer the consequences later on as we go along. But I prepared you from the very beginning: I will not tolerate any games. Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in that case, may I ask for a 15-minute break to try to contact the lead counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm slightly concerned about what you just said in relation to Madam Fauveau. If you say that she has not been given permission to represent him, then effectively today he is unrepresented, which -- it may be that none of Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination touches upon that but nonetheless, it seems to me that--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't say that she is not being given permission. I said that I have been advised not to give her permission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour is content for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For today, yes, but I also recall, and I'm sure that Ms. Fauveau will remember Mr. De Roux's statement last Wednesday -- I don't know if you were here or not. I suppose you were here, if my memory doesn't fail me, but he specifically said that he will be absent for medical reasons today, and today only. Now you come forward this morning and you tell us that he is not going to be here, something that we knew already; that you are going to ask to represent General Talic today, something that we were prepared for already and to which General Talic had given his consent way back even on last Wednesday. But now we are also informed that he will not be here today -- tomorrow, that Mr. Pitron is not here today and he will not be here tomorrow, that Monday, none of them will be here. And then Tuesday, we will be honoured by the presence of one or the other. We still don't even know whether they will be both here or will only -- there will only be Maitre de Roux here. We will not tolerate that situation to prevail. No way. You can rest assured that when I say I mean business, I mean business. I will not tolerate any games, any tactics. I will certainly not allow, if this is the intention of the Defence - it's certainly not yours - but if it is even remotely the intention of using this methodology as a stratagem for later on creating problems for the Trial Chamber, forget it. I will never give you the chance, even the slightest chance. And if you need 15 minutes, I will give you even 30 minutes to consult with Maitre de Roux, but make it clear that at the end of this -- today's sitting, we are coming down with a ruling. If the situation is the same tomorrow. There will be a further ruling. If the situation is even worse on Monday, then I think Maitre de Roux and Maitre Pitron should know what the final decision is going to be. The sitting is suspended for a further half an hour -- 15 minutes. --- Break taken at 11.04 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mademoiselle Fauveau. Wait until the two accused are seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. de Roux, the lead counsel for General Talic has informed me that he has just made a request to the Registry, in accordance with General Talic, that I be designated counsel for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I hope Maitre de Roux does not think that that solves the whole problem. I hope Maitre de Roux knows that Maitre Michel Pitron is not yet officially recognised as co-counsel, for the simple reason that for six months, he has kept this office waiting for the documentation that was required of him or requested of him. I'm fully confident that you have ample qualifications and perhaps as qualified, if not more, to be co-counsel yourself. But it doesn't mean to say that we can go on like this. Just to make myself clear, or clearer, what I said before is not to be intended as meaning that you do not have the right here, once you belong to a defence team, to stand up and make representations on behalf of General Talic or conduct cross-examination, if necessary, or put some questions, if necessary. But this should be the exception and not the rule. The rule is that once this Tribunal has appointed one person, and unofficially recognises a second person as being the defence team for General Talic, that's the yardstick that we have to stick by. I am sorry, I mean, I will -- I would have loved not to embarrass you. I have two daughters. I don't like speaking to anyone the way I had to speak this morning, especially being more or less very direct and somewhat rough. I hope you understand that this is due to the frustration that this Trial Chamber finds itself in. I mean, please do realise, and this is why we are going to take action, that Maitre Pitron, in spite of the fact that he has kept this -- the Registry of this Tribunal waiting for six months to send over the documentation that was requested of him, and he hasn't sent it, only had the decency to appear, show up, twice in 12 -- in the 12 sittings that we've had. And Maitre de Roux, the lead counsel, has showed up 50 per cent, six times, while you are here every day and you have to -- I'm afraid you have to shoulder all the responsibility on your own, bear with me, and also with the frustration of this Trial Chamber. It's not fair on you, it's not fair on us, it's not fair on General Talic, and we will not allow it to go on. Again, we believe, and obviously General Talic agrees to it, that you are perfectly capable defend him and that when you are defending him, he is in good hands, but he also has a right to have the two lawyers that have been - one officially and the other one semi-officially - assigned to him to be present, either one or the other or both. So I think that closes the chapter for the moment. We will hand out the ruling just the same, later on. Please tell Maitre de Roux that I do not accept half measures. Unfortunately, Maitre de Roux and myself haven't had any previous occasions of working together. I hope he takes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the message.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. And Your Honours, he has received your message. Unfortunately, he is just being admitted to hospital and I'm afraid he will not be discharged before Monday. If he is discharged earlier, he will be here on Monday, but certainly on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he must have known this last Wednesday. Last Wednesday he specifically said, please allow me to absent myself on Wednesday -- on Tuesday of next week. That was yesterday. And we were very forthcoming. We said okay. But that was yesterday, and today is today, and Monday will be Monday, and we go on and I have learned not to take risks and to expect anything. So I will always be prepared. I was in the Boy Scouts when I was a tiny tot and I have learned that maxim first and foremost, "be prepared." So let's go on. Mr. Ackerman will continue his cross-examination after the witness is brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During the break, perhaps while the witness is coming in, the Court asked me to clear up the matter of the two different translations. The witness will now have in front of him the same translation Mr. Ackerman has. While I'm not 100 per cent sure, I believe I figured out what the problem was. It appears that this statement from 1995 appeared as part of the supporting materials. When the accused are brought in, these are translated, and they are normally redacted to omit certain information that could identify the witness. Then apparently the statement was translated again as part of a witness statement. So there are two different translations in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- just one simple question. The document that he had in front of him before, was it signed by him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the answer that I wanted from you. I couldn't make that comment myself when I had it in front of me. I just -- but the one he has now is signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No. No B/C/S translation is ever signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is ever signed, but that's the one that's read out to him, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not even?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The English is read out to him and translated orally. There is an oral interpretation of the statement by whichever person is with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So neither of the B/C/S versions is signed. Which is not wise, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've had slightly longer, not a lot longer but slightly longer here than Mr. Koumjian. I think Your Honour may have got slightly confused by the fact that the Rule 92 B/C/S version is in fact signed but when statements were taken originally, and this has been thought about very often, it was too complicated to transcribe it in the original version because the investigator didn't know what was in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But so, as Mr. Koumjian says, the statement is taken by way of an interpreter, written down in English. At the end, it's read back by either the same interpreter or sometimes a different. So one of the major problems, and this has come up before in a number of trials, is it is very difficult to say that this is a statement of the accused for those reasons -- of the witness, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of the witness, not of the accused. Thanks for the information, Ms. Korner. Let's go ahead, Mr. Krzic. Mr. Ackerman will now continue with his cross-examination. In the meantime, we have sort of, I am informed, cleared the problem that we had before, that is the apparent discrepancy between the document you had in front of you and the document that Mr. Ackerman had in his possession. I don't know if you were following what was being said by Mr. Koumjian and Ms. Korner just now. I suppose the next thing is to look at the document, see if there is now that short sentence in B/C/S or in Serbo-Croat, saying, "I call," or "I call him collaborator," and perhaps furnish Mr. Ackerman with your reaction to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean my reaction to what you have said or to the words that Mr. Ackerman mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, your reaction to Mr. Ackerman's question, that is explanation that he asked from you regarding that particular sentence, where supposedly, you say that you call or called him a collaborator while previously, during your testimony of about an hour ago, you said that you never said that he was a collaborator.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is such a minute detail that it is very difficult to respond. If I did say that, I may have said it under emotional pressure, and I abide by the fact that Mr. Islamovic did not agree for other SDA members to attend this important meeting, the delegation to attend, and it may have been that my angry response could have included such a term, because it was unacceptable for me for a deputy of the SDA, a member of the executive board of the SDA, to refuse to appear together with us at such an important assignment, whereas on the other hand, he obeyed the president of the assembly or the municipality who already then was on the side of the current authorities, which we considered at the time to be usurpers. So as not to bind me by the words I used, I used "usurper. " What I meant was "occupying authorities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, let me see if we can just sort of clear this issue in a way that will make it possible for to us deal with it more easily in the future. If you'll go back to the English version of your first statement at page 15, please. This is the one between 27 December, 1994 and 23 August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fifteen. This was a statement that was taken to you over quite a long period of time, days in December of 1994, March, April, May and August of 1995. At some point, there was a -- this written version that we have in front of us was prepared, and at some point, at the bottom of page 15, you affixed your signature, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you read the English version before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For careful reading, one needs time and those were circumstances -- to tell you the truth, these statements that I made, I didn't consider each and every bit of it to be raised in Court. If I conveyed my intimate feelings, I never thought that that could be the object of a trial. I thought that facts would be addressed at trial, facts that influence, but let me stop there. Let me not elaborate. So let me repeat once again, it is possible that in the heat of the moment, I have -- I may have said that, because he put himself in that position. If somebody wants to act alone, without his party colleagues being present, then on the other hand, he's been invited to attend by the occupying powers, you can make your own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Koumjian, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I was just going to ask the Chamber to ask Mr. Krzic to limit his answer to the question. The question was whether he read the statement before he signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which he had answered, too, earlier as well this morning. He had already stated that he had.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably read it but the signing and the reading of the statement took place very quickly. Yes, absolutely, I did have a chance to read it. Now, how much attention I devoted to it is another matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that you really weren't concerned about whether or not the statement was accurate, that you thought that was unimportant?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I thought that what I was saying was being literally conveyed, or verbatim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you might have called him a collaborator because you were under pressure. At the time you were giving your statement to the investigators from the OTP, who was putting you under pressure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, one moment. That's why I asked the witness specifically at the point in time to tell me whether that statement in B/C/S is in the past tense or in the present tense, because if it is in the present tense, your question makes sense. If it's in the past tense, as it was translated to us by the interpreters while he was reading it, then your question doesn't make sense or doesn't follow, or should not be tolerated. Please, Mr. Krzic, look at the statement in your language, in the Serbo-Croat language, that particular sentence, which was -- which you were asked to read out earlier on. Could you please tell me, or tell us, whether that is in the present tense or in the past tense? Do you mean to sigh that then, on that occasion, you called Mr. Islamovic a collaborator or that you now are telling the investigators or the persons interviewing you that you consider him a collaborator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I called him, at that point in time, that as a reaction to his failure to respect relationships within a political party. Instead, he respected a representative of a political party which at the time was exerting oppression against the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ackerman, I suppose you should move to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- in your -- we are back to your, I think it's your third statement. It's the one of December 2000 and February 2001 and we are back on page 4. Near the bottom of that statement, you said that you didn't know if Banja Luka had two Crisis Staffs operating simultaneously. My question is: Do you now know that there were in fact a municipal Crisis Staff and a Regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you now know that Mr. Brdjanin was never a member of the municipal Crisis Staff but only the Regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether I know. Logically, he should not have been a member of the municipal Crisis Staff, but in those days, that does not exclude his presence, and I'm not claiming that he was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6 of that statement, near the bottom, the short paragraph right before the last paragraph, you were talking about reports you would receive from people about things that were going on outside Banja Luka, and you say that, on occasions, you were not able to double check the information to see if it was accurate but had to rely on what one person or so might have told you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please -- I can't find that page. I don't know which one -- which version you're talking about, the English or Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the English version, page 6 --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you said 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I probably did. The paragraph at the bottom starts with, "Many times Bosniaks living outside Banja Luka." Do you see that sentence? I think you might be looking at a different statement than I am.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the full statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Follow me. It's the one before the last of your statements. It's the statement which was the result of the interviews that took place between the 10th and the 14th of December, 2000 and then the 10th, the 12th, the 14th and the 15th of February of last year, of 2001. The part he -- Mr. Ackerman is referring to has got a short title, a title, which is called "Valter." In the English version, it's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Find the 2001 statement. It has the date 2001 on the front. It's probably number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It should be number 3, yeah. It should be statement number 3. And if you have found it, the part with the title.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's the sixth paragraph from the title. It starts, "Many times, Bosniaks living outside Banja Luka." Mr. Ackerman wants to know whether what you allegedly state there is correct or not, or whether you stand by it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have since found out, have you not, that sometimes the stories you were told turned out later not to have been true, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some not entirely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention on page 7 in the second paragraph, that begins, "In 1994," you are referring to members and a group, and I assume this was your SDA group that was working together. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't members of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't all members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you referring to when you refer to your group?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were people whom I would see. I often spoke to them and exchanged information with them, and after my departure from Banja Luka, these people continued to see each other in various places and they participated in the work of humanitarian organisations, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that there was a member of that group who had an axe to grind against you, who provided some false information apparently; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that that had the axe to grind against you that provided false information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
