utterances.text: Could I just, Your Honour, object and ask what the relevance of this would be? If there is some relevance, I can see going into it but otherwise we are asking the witness in a public international forum to get into matters that may cause him some personal problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, what is the relevance of this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he wants to say the name in closed session, I have no problem with that but it would make it possible for us to investigate the veracity of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if you finish reading that same paragraph, the one on page 7, starting, "In 1994," which I am not inviting you to read out loud, there is the explanation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you're right, Your Honour. I just saw it. I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now going to page 10. With all these reports that were being made to you by people from outside Banja Luka, you were getting the impression, weren't you, that some bad things were happening to Muslim people outside Banja Luka in the region of the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what does the word "ARK" mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of these things that we were learning that were apparently going on outside Banja Luka were things that you were reporting to the media and to various governments outside the former Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the media. I provided information to the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- but you tried to keep that information from the non-Serb population in Banja Luka for fear that it would spread panic amongst them, forcing them to flee the area, something that you didn't want to happen. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confidential statements that might have a negative influence, negative consequences, when we are talking about such statements, it is obvious that they could not be made public, especially since the dissemination of such information has certain consequences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you could have shared it with your fellow Muslims in Banja Luka, couldn't you, without having made it public. There was a way for you to do that, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at page 10 of your statement, the next to the last paragraph on the page begins with the language, "We never shared." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We never shared our information with the local non-Serb population in Banja Luka, especially we never told them about the killings that had happened in the region. Giving such information would have spread panic amongst them, forcing non-Serbs to flee, something we did not wanted." It probably should be "want." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the non-Serb locals, I think that a mistake has been made and the translation, it is correct, the non-Serbian population of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. How did you arrive at the decision to try to keep from these people what was really happening to keep them from leaving the area as opposed to warning them that it might be best for them to leave the area because of the danger that appeared to be approaching? In other words, why didn't you start assisting them to try to get away from what appeared to you to be a dangerous situation, instead of not giving the information, and keeping them there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population was well aware of what was happening because they would listen to foreign news, especially the Voice of America, Zagreb, and even Sarajevo. Providing special information, the information that we obtained, would have revealed the source and it would have also revealed that we were those who provided that information, sending it on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So efforts you made to keep this information from the local non-Serb population were not effective, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question really is why would you decide to hide this kind of information in an effort to keep people from fleeing if you believed that serious danger was coming and that they were in great danger? You told the reporter Veronique at about that time that you thought 200.000 people would be killed if war came, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I provided information to the entire population, even to the non-Serbian population. I provided this information in some of my numerous interviews. You can find this in my book, too. I explained in detail what was happening in this information. This can be confirmed by three journalists. It was confirmed by three journalists in their books. In the Hotel Bosna, I publicly, not just myself but my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. collaborators too, I spoke in public about the concentration camps before about 50 people. I won't go into details. It concerns a lot of material. So this is not true. But it was not possible to provide all the information except at press conferences, and here in these cases it was necessary to be cautious in case -- with regard to the crimes and the pressure and everything that we have spoken about here, this was made public and it is known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remained in Banja Luka throughout the entire year 1992 and into the year -- well into the year 1993, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, you were asked the question about how it was that someone so vocal about what was going on there could have possibly survived in such an environment. If you look at page 15 of this statement that we are looking at, it's the paragraph in the middle of the page right before you change to a new ERN number, about halfway through, you indicate that you can only speculate about how you managed to survive but that you believe the Serb authorities on purpose refrained from getting high-ranking Bosniak and Croat officials killed because such killings would have drawn unnecessary attention in the media. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of that paragraph, you also indicated your belief that Karadzic or the Serb authorities in Banja Luka were put on notice that no harm should come to you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was under this impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put on notice by whom? Who did you think had told them not to harm you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speculate about that. This was something that I felt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it you thought, though, had put pressure on them not to harm you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can confirm is Mr. Vance's statement with regard to the event in question, to the effect that the people who spoke to him could always contact him for protection through his secretary or through the Security Council, so perhaps this is what made me think that -- that such a thing was possible, that it was possible to make such a request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suspect if he could have had that impact, Mr. Vance would have requested that nobody be harmed, wouldn't you think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, don't answer this question, please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 17, you speak in the second full paragraph that begins with the words, "The SDA members." You speak of two Bosniaks from Banja Luka who collaborated with Serbs in the municipal assembly, Adem Gunic and Nedzad Kusmic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicate that you gave them orders to leave the government and they refused to do so. In early 1992, you gave them such orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it they were collaborating and what were they doing that you believe was collaboration?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I must remind you that all of our deputies left the municipal assembly and very soon HDZ deputies did so, too, on a permanent basis. The reason for this was that we were not -- we could not allow anyone to be present in such a structure, given that there were mass crimes being committed around us and that such crimes were being committed in Banja Luka. There was nothing we could do in the organs of the authorities and being present in these government authorities could only mean that support was being given for this. I'm talking about explanations. These were members of the SDA party and it was their duty to listen to the decision of the executive committee. This was not my decision. If at the municipal assembly were such discriminatory decisions were taken and the Vice-President, the former Vice-President of the municipal assembly, says nothing, nothing at all, in our eyes, this amounted to collaboration. It amounted to an unexpressed form of collaboration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us long ago, on the first day you came here, that one of the tenets of the SDA was to create and support democratic institutions, to support democracy, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it's democratic for members of a minority party in a legislature who don't get their way to simply walk out of the legislature?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't answer the question now. Your objection, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Argumentative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's argumentative. It's just a question as to whether he thinks that's democratic or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why should he be asked to make a statement on this? It was a political decision that was taken at that level, at his level at the time and it's not a question -- it has got nothing to do with democracy and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I won't insist on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Don't answer the question. Your motion is overruled, thank you. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a time, was there not Mr. Krzic, when you gave a series of interviews to Edina Kamenica of Oslobodjenje newspaper in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have described her as a very renowned journalist, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She, in fact, was the assistant editor of that newspaper, was she not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Your stated purpose for granting an interview, these interviews, was because in your words, you said you were being -- you were wrongly being implicated in what had happened, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know what you are reading but if you want me to provide you with the right interpretation of what you are reading, you have to tell me where this can be found. If you want me to tell you what my opinion of this is right now, and I think it differs, I will be glad to reply to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at page 18 at the -- near the bottom of the page, the paragraph begins, "At the time of these interviews." And it continues, "The situation in Sarajevo was very confusing. There were many obscure groups there. A lot of information about Banja Luka that was not true was in circulation. I had got the impression that I was wrongly being implicated in what had happened in Banja Luka." That's what you said, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And part of your reason for giving this interview was to clear that up so that you would no longer be implicated in what had happened in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons, and the other reason was, as I have said, with regard to myself, this also concerned several other people who were also at that time in the free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This interview was not well received by many Muslim people. You were you criticised pretty heavily for this interview, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not accused of doing great harm to the Muslim people by this interview?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the interview, if you look at this, your statement here beginning on page 18, what you're doing, are you not, is describing some of the things that you said in that interview and explaining them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, for instance, you said in the interview that during the attack in Kozarac, that there were Muslim aggressors, correct? It's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the -- I received information that there were Muslims in the Serbian army, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was your explanation of what you meant when you said in that interview that there were Muslim aggressors

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the fighters of Vecici, you said in the interview that you had a certain role to play in their escape to Travnik, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 5. The quote is, "I had a certain role to play in their escape to Travnik." And then you go on to explain that you didn't physically help them but you provided them with good advice. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To avoid speculation, my advice was that it related to the presence of the International Red Cross and to foreign journalists, which that's not true, it can be seen here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of that, talking about the acquisition of weapons by the Muslims, what you apparently said in your interview was, "Don't ask how we managed it. We even got it from the Serbs." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On page 20, you begin talking about the book you wrote. When did you write this book?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in Norway, while I was staying there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the years that that was done?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there from the end of 1994, 1994, until the autumn of 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you'll look at page 21 of your statement, referring to page 104, I guess it is, of the English translation of your book, and according to what I'm looking at, you refer to a person by the name of Radovan Brdjanin. Is that a mistake or did you not know his name at that point?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a very simple explanation. I often confused the name of Vukic and the name of Brdjanin. So it wasn't really in my ear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they are both named Radoslav, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that to the investigators. I continued to call him Radovan although the name was, in fact, Radoslav.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You speak on page 22 of a meeting that you had in Prijedor with SDA leaders from Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa, Jajce and Kljuc. In your book you apparently say that Mujagic, while describing the status of preparations in Prijedor, stated that they had over 2.000 barrels and even a small cannon, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2.000 barrels, meaning long guns or rifles, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And pistols and hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These meetings, like this one, of the SDA leaders from these various municipalities, were coordinated by the Bosanska Krajina SDA, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at page 23, you speak of a meeting that was held in Zenica. About halfway down the page, it starts with -- the paragraph starts with, "On page 18," "a meeting that was held in Zenica, attended by all the regions to review the data on armaments. In that meeting the military council of the Patriotic League was astounded by the data for they were surprised at the reported numbers and assessed that the Bosnian Krajina was in a better position than other regions for mounting a resistance to the expected aggression." Yes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I received this information from a man who was a participant, but I didn't ask specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when you received the information?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994 -- sorry, sorry. I beg your pardon. It could have been 1996. When I started writing my book, I started inquiring about some other things, and so I asked this person about this. The person who should have known, to what extent this person conveyed the information to me correctly, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the real definitions because I did not belong to the Patriotic League, formally or informally. I can tell you what I learned later on. During my stay in Banja Luka, I hardly heard about the Patriotic League at all and at the meetings that we had, and you asked me a moment ago about that meeting. I don't remember that there was any reference to the Patriotic League. So that my statement as to what the Patriotic League meant when I learnt about it in 1995 and 1996, I think would be quite irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what the Patriotic League was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that in those days that you're asking me about, I didn't know exactly what the Patriotic League was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know what the military council of the Patriotic League was either?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the fall of 1991, Sefer Halilovic came to Banja Luka, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, he was with the Patriotic League, the leader of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I didn't know him in person, nor did I know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The topic of discussion at that meeting was how to protect Bosniaks in Banja Luka in case war were to break out?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you tell us in your statement that in that meeting about how to protect Bosniaks in Banja Luka in case war were to break out, you never discussed weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, because as you will see, there were no activities that ensued after that. Therefore, as far as I was concerned, it was a completely -- or a fruitless meeting, as far as your question is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that Sefer Halilovic was a former JNA officer, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt that later in Sarajevo, in 1994. Until then, I repeat, I didn't even know the man's name. He probably introduced himself and gave a name but I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Sefer Halilovic, who had been an officer in the JNA and became the commanding general of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, came and met with you in Banja Luka and never mentioned that he had any military experience, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him mentioning it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose of the meeting was how to protect Bosniaks in Banja Luka in case of war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it you talk about when you talk about protecting people in case of war, if you don't talk about weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a natural reflex was that in a state of war there would be no medicines, it would not be possible to ensure food supplies, and that efforts should be made to provide reserve supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time there was an expectation that there was going to be a war, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a rumour that even appeared in the press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of ideas, other than what you've mentioned, did people at that meeting come up with as ways to protect Bosniaks in case of war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, there were discussions about organising teams of physicians, in particular, and I mentioned that Dr. Hadziagic was in charge of the question of medicines, bandages. That was all that was discussed. And I must say that at the time, and after that, and even today, I was very disappointed by such an attitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This meeting with General Halilovic was in the fall of 1991. In February of 1992, you then go to Sarajevo for the purpose of obtaining weapons, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I think it was in March, but I would have to look it up in my notes. I think it was in March that I was in Sarajevo at a public meeting that reviewed the current situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially from the point of view of international relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, let me interrupt you. It's my assumption that you would like to finish your testimony and go home this week. Is that a fair assumption?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't let yourself be carried away with that, Mr. Krzic. What Mr. Ackerman means is what I told you earlier on: Answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question, because otherwise you'll be asking for trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the question I asked you was fairly simple, and let me help you. If you look at the bottom of page 23, you say, "My visit to Sarajevo in February of 1992, the purpose was to obtain weapons." My only question is: That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fairness to you, what you then said was that you were only able to obtain two weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You expected to obtain many more than that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just then, but later. Of course, I personally could not have carried such weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also during this period, April through December of 1992, sometime during that period, there was a SDA Crisis Staff, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had one. That was exclusively concerned with humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the top of page 25, you say that at one meeting, you were criticised by some young men for not advising the press that the Bosniaks had been armed, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same page, you speak of a person named Salih as someone who transported arms around Banja Luka in preparation for a possible fight, and at the time you made the statement you had forgotten his last name. Have you remembered who he was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still cannot remember the surname just now but I have to correct you, by saying that I even gave my own weapon to him because weapons were transported to the places where more intensive attacks were expected on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. homes and families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave him the weapon that you had gotten in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you told the OTP investigator during this statement that you threw it in the Vrbas River, that wasn't correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I had another pistol, a number 9, which hadn't been registered, and I had a registered Bereta, which I didn't throw away, but the police seized it from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us that the weapon you got in Sarajevo, you gave to Salih. Do you want to change that or do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say now which of the two I gave to him and which I threw away, but in any event, I got rid of both so that they wouldn't be on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was easy for you two minutes ago to say that you gave it to Salih. Now it's difficult for you to say what happened to it. Is that because you had previously said and forgotten that you had said that you threw it in the river?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, the frequency and the danger was such that if you ask me about such a detail, one would have to think it over and look back to that period. One needs to refresh one's memory, and you're now skipping from one subject to another and it is very difficult to concentrate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I hope you understand that what's going on here is important and serious, and I hope you would understand that you should not answer questions if you're not certain that your answer is correct, and if you need to reflect back, then do so. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that one of the weapons -- I did give one of the weapons to Salih, and I'm also certain that I threw one of the weapons into the Vrbas River. On one occasion, I went to the Vrbas riverbank and saw a barrel close by and some other people were digging, burying their weapons and throwing them away, so...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you to page 26. The Vecici fighters were receiving weapons from Salih, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Salih, you appear to imply that there was a warehouse of weapons that was transported by trucks. It is quite possible that Salih gave one or several weapons to someone. I really couldn't know that, nor did I want to know it at the time, because knowledge of that kind would not only expose you to danger but also those who were actually doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what you in fact said was you don't know the exact number of weapons the fighters in Vecici received from Salih, and that's still the case, isn't it? You still don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told us, or it's in your statement, that the Vecici fighters destroyed a number of armoured vehicles and killed 70 Chetniks. That would take some fairly sophisticated weaponry to do that, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the statement of the people of Vecici, and you can find out to what extent it is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't destroy armoured vehicles with hunting rifles, do you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With hand-held rocket launchers or even with hand grenades, as far as I know, or with mines, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, where do we stand with your cross-examination? How much more do you think you have? How much more time, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm telling you why. I'll tell you why. Because I need a short break to finish the ruling that we have to give, to which I referred to earlier. That would be the last act for today. Little time, that means I need a quarter of an hour. We also need to break in any case because I would imagine that the interpreters are waiting for that kind of good news, and possibly I wouldn't like to stop you when you would prefer to go on or when you still have a chapter to open. So if you could direct me on that, give me an idea, then we can follow up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears, it's very difficult. The witness I think is starting to answer a little more quickly now so I think we can move a little faster, but I would guess a couple of hours. I've got -- you can see it there on the end of the table, a stack of exhibits. I don't expect to have the witness discuss every one of those exhibits but, most of them, I want to bring his attention to statements that are contained within them. I think it can be wrapped up in a couple of hours. I hope so. That's my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, okay. So I'm giving you until quarter -- let me ask the interpreters, first, whether they prefer to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I expected that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Fairly direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will break now. You will resume, that will be -- you will have roughly 15 minutes to 20 minutes to wrap up this particular part of your cross-examination, with the understanding that you will of course continue tomorrow, and that would leave us with just about five minutes to give the ruling. So we'll stop now and resume at quarter past 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. I apologise to everyone, having taken longer than I had anticipated. Mr. Ackerman, I ask for your indulgence. It's 1.35 now. Shall we adjourn your examination for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for your cooperation. Perhaps we could ask Mr. Krzic in so we explain to him because I think we owe him also kind of an apology. Mr. Krzic, please. Tomorrow, the understanding is that everyone will do his or her best to conclude with Mr. Krzic. You have, I understand, about two hours. Then there will be re-examination. Do you expect to have a long re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not long but some, a short re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say that the first hour this morning covered what I believe was ten minutes worth of cross-examination. I'm going to try really hard tomorrow and I think I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Krzic, you may sit down. Good afternoon, Mr. Krzic. The Trial Chamber has already said how sorry we all are that it took us longer before we could reconvene. Unfortunately, as things are and the hour being what it is, since we have to vacate this courtroom by -- in a very short while, I think we owe an apology to you as well for having kept you waiting outside, thinking that there would be a continuation of the cross-examination this morning. That's not going to happen. We are very sorry but we were kept away because we had to draft an important ruling. I'm afraid, in any case, you were going to come again tomorrow so we will finish with you tomorrow. Mr. Ackerman will finish his cross-examination and then there will be a re-examination and maybe one or two questions from the bench if that is necessary. And again, once more, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mademoiselle Fauveau, I would like to clear two things with you before we proceed with the ruling. You stated earlier on that on Tuesday of next week, Maitre de Roux will be showing up. Did you also say, because we sort of are not exactly 100 per cent sure of this, did you just mention Maitre de Roux or also Maitre Pitron?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maitre de Roux will be here on Tuesday. Maitre Pitron will certainly be here on Wednesday and he might be here on Tuesday. I don't know yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second question I wanted to ask was when you mentioned that Monday next, there will be a -- some development in a sense of a request to the Registry, to the Registrar, for the allocation of a co-counsel, were you referring to yourself as being nominated or something that has to do with Maitre Pitron to regularise his position?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a situation at the beginning of the day, and it was a question of Maitre Pitron. I then spoke to Maitre de Roux, who said that he had submitted a request, according to which I should be appointed as co-counsel, so this is nothing to do with Maitre Pitron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I thank you, Mademoiselle Fauveau. So Madam Registrar, please, the Trial Chamber is going to give an oral ruling. It will be reduced in written form later on, but if I show it to you now, it looks like a Chagall. The Trial Chamber notes that in the course of the sitting of Wednesday, February 6, Maitre Xavier de Roux, counsellor for accused General Momir Talic, informed the Trial Chamber that for personal, medical reasons, he will be -- he will not be in a position to attend for today's sitting during which co-counsel, Maitre Michel Pitron, will also be absent. Note that in the course of today's sitting, Mademoiselle Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic informed the Trial Chamber that until next Tuesday, February 19, 2002, the position will remain unchanged, and that as a consequence, she prayed that this Trial Chamber authorises her to represent General Momir Talic. Notes further that in the sitting of Wednesday, February 6, General Momir Talic, upon a prompt from Maitre de Roux, entered a declaration to the effect that he accepted to be represented by Mademoiselle Fauveau during the absence of Maitre Xavier de Roux, which, however, as already pointed out, was meant to be restricted to yesterday's sitting only. Notes, the statement made earlier on in today's sitting by the Prosecutor to the effect that on Monday, February 18, a witness is expected to be brought forward and who will be testifying on a direct encounter he or she had with accused General Momir Talic. Notes that although Maitre Michel Pitron is not yet on record as co-counsel, he is acknowledged by the Registrar to be acting in that capacity temporarily and is further being paid for his appearances, and that this also automatically entails responsibility vis-a-vis the accused General Momir Talic as well as vis-a-vis this Tribunal. Notes further that his official appointment as co-counsel has been delayed pending his furnishing the Registrar of this Tribunal with the documentation that was asked of him months ago. Notes that Maitre Michel Pitron has been absent from this courtroom for the past two weeks at least and has not provided this Trial Chamber with an indication as to when his return is to be expected, save what has just been stated by Mademoiselle Fauveau upon being questioned ad hoc by this Trial Chamber. Notes further that Maitre Xavier de Roux, during last Wednesday's, February 6, sitting, stated that he will be unable to put an appearance during today's sitting for personal medical reasons and it was for this purpose only, for this reason only, that this Trial Chamber authorised him to absent himself, and only for yesterday's sitting. Notes further that the information given to the Trial Chamber in the course of today's sitting assumes that this absence of Maitre de Roux will, as stated earlier, extend until Tuesday, February 19. Notes that since this trial started there have been, including today's sitting, 12 sittings in all and Maitre de Roux failed to put in an appearance at half of them while his co-counsel Maitre Pitron only showed up for two sittings. Notes that during the totality of the second week of this trial, both Maitre de Roux and Maitre Pitron were absent without even furnishing an explanation, let alone a justification for their absence. Notes further that accused General Talic himself confirmed that, as regards that particular week and the absence of his counsel during the same, he had not been given any information by the same counsel, at not being contacted by them. Considering that this situation cannot be allowed to go on and it is imperative for this Trial Chamber to ensure that the rights of accused General Talic be protected while the obligations of counsel appointed to defend him are fully met, more especially so in the circumstances mentioned by the Prosecution earlier on in this sitting. Considering further that the Trial Chamber is duty bound to ensure that this trial proceeds regularly without any obstacles, directs lead council Maitre Xavier de Roux and co-counsel Maitre Michel Pitron to ensure their presence at this trial without further delay in accordance with the obligations assumed vis-a-vis their client and this Tribunal. The matter, at the moment, I am leaving. We are leaving this matter as it is. We will take it up again more forcefully if the situation does not improve, and when I say more forcefully, I am -- I might have easily used the word "terminally." That is what the Trial Chamber has in mind. So.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just correct one thing for the purposes of clarity? Your Honour, on the LiveNote at page 66, line 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour referred to M de Roux's absence being restricted to yesterday's sitting. It is in fact today's sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my mistake. [Microphone not activated] Yes, you are right, Ms. Korner, that is what the Trial Chamber meant to say. Definitely. You are 100 per cent right. In fact, actually, we resumed today so that was what was meant. I am sure, Mademoiselle Fauveau, you understand the situation and that you will carry the message to your colleagues and that the situation will improve, failing which please do remember and do take into consideration that the fact that I have your assurance that Maitre de Roux assured you that he has made a request for you to be taken on board does not solve the position. It's not a question on whether General Talic can ably and sufficiently well be defended by you. That has never been the issue. The issue is something completely different. And the Trial Chamber certainly cannot wait until the situation is clarified the way Maitre de Roux is suggesting that it be clarified, in other words by your addition to Pitron, Maitre Pitron, or to your replacement of Mr. Pitron. That is -- that would not be a situation which we can tolerate. Obviously, we will take it into consideration but taking it into consideration does not mean that Maitre de Roux, as lead counsel, has carte blanche to rely on you or on Maitre Pitron irrespective of whether he's going to exert control on Maitre Pitron to be present here to fulfil his obligations. I think I have made myself clear. Don't expect us to relax on this. So the message is very clear. We are going to move forward if necessary and to proceed with the matter, if necessary. I'm sorry this took up a substantial portion of today's sitting. I am sure that you as lawyers understand that this constitutes a preoccupation in the minds of the three judges composing this Trial Chamber. I wouldn't have been able to sleep peacefully tonight if I had not brought it up, and what disturbed me was actually your immediate first statement, first thing in the morning, that we are not going to have Maitre de Roux until Tuesday next at least. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood what you said. It was very clear. However, I think that I and my office, Maitre de Roux and Maitre Pitron, will take what you have said very seriously and I'm sure that this will be solved as of next Monday. However, I think I might have a problem tomorrow because Maitre de Roux is in hospital. I'm sure of that. And Maitre Pitron, I was unable to contact him so I'm not sure that Maitre Pitron will be able to be here tomorrow. I will do all I can to ensure that he is present but I cannot guarantee this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mademoiselle Fauveau, the Trial Chamber does not hold you responsible for ensuring that either Maitre de Roux or Maitre Pitron show up. It's definitely not your responsibility. It's their responsibility to show up. So in other words, to us this problem does not exist. I assume that you will be here tomorrow. It's no major harm in view because more or less what's going to happen tomorrow is Mr. Ackerman will finish his cross-examination. Then there will be a re-examination, I understand a brief one, maybe a couple of questions, and then we will review some of the points that were raised during the informal meeting that my senior -- our senior legal officer had with you last week, just to make sure that there is an understanding which we -- on several issues which we will formalise here. Obviously, if you have difficulties at that point in time, you will have the full understanding of the Trial Chamber, but the more difficulties you will have, the more strengthened will be the determination of the Trial Chamber to proceed with what it has in mind of doing should a solution not be found. Yes, I am being told by Madam Registrar that I have overstepped all the limits that were expected of us. I thank you all. Again my apologise for, not wasting but for whatever happened, and we will continue tomorrow. We will resume at 9.00 sharp and hopefully we will finish with the witness by the end of the morning. I thank you.
